title: Drawing It So People Understand
gist: However good the idea, nobody funds or builds what they can't picture. Representational consistency, semantic layers, three standards worth knowing, and the antipattern that makes architects defend bad diagrams.
minute: **Representational consistency**: always show the relationship between parts before changing the view. Whole topology → where the part sits → the part in detail.

Use drawing **layers semantically**. Base layer = topology, and it says *synchronous*, not *gRPC*. Next layer = implementation. Further layers = DDD boundaries, transaction scope, whatever you want to contrast.

Three standards: **UML** (class and sequence diagrams survived; the rest didn't), **C4** (Context, Container, Component, Class — the modern default), **ArchiMate** (enterprise scope, deliberately minimal).
The one near-universal convention: **solid lines are synchronous, dotted lines are asynchronous**. Almost nothing else about shapes is standard, so build your own set and publish a key.
**Irrational Artifact Attachment**: your attachment to an artifact is proportional to how long it took to make. Stay low-fidelity early, so you can throw things away.

sections.alt: A whole topology, then the same topology with one part highlighted, then that part in detail
sections.cap: Fig. 23-1 · three frames, and the middle one is the one people skip.
sections.p: To explain how the Silicon Sandwiches plug-ins relate to each other, you start with the whole topology, then show the relationship between it and the plug-in structure, and only then the plug-in structure itself. **Showing a portion without its place in the whole confuses viewers** — and it is a source of confusion you can eliminate for free.

sections.t: You spent four hours making the diagram beautiful
sections.alt: Attachment plotted against hours spent producing an artifact, rising steeply
sections.sit: You built a careful architecture diagram in a proper tool. In review, someone proposes a change that would invalidate the structure you drew. You find yourself explaining why the current design is fine.
opts: This is **Irrational Artifact Attachment** — attachment proportional to production time. Four hours in Visio makes you twice as attached as two hours would have. The design isn't being defended on its merits.
Work in low-fidelity artifacts until the team has iterated enough.
A whiteboard photo, index cards, sticky notes. Cheap enough to throw away, which is what frees people to experiment and lets the real shape emerge through revision and argument.
sections.verdict: Eventually you *do* need the nice diagram in the fancy tool — just not before the team has iterated on the design. Many architects have replaced the whiteboard with a **tablet on a projector**: unlimited canvas, copy-paste for “what if” variants that would obscure the original, already digitised without the photograph glare, and it works with people who aren't in the room.

sections.alt: Three stacked planes: topology at the base, implementation above it, context overlays on top
sections.cap: What to look for in a diagramming tool — and how to use the most important feature properly.
items: **Layers** — group items logically and show or hide them. Build a comprehensive diagram and hide the detail until you're discussing it, or reveal a picture incrementally through a presentation.

**Stencils and templates** — a library of common visual components, including composites. Building a stencil set for the patterns your organisation uses gives consistency across every diagram and makes new ones faster.
**Magnets** — the points on a shape where connecting lines snap. Small feature, large effect on whether diagrams look considered.
sections.p: The layer discipline is the part worth internalising: **the base layer is architecture, not implementation**. It should say *synchronous communication*, not name a protocol. Implementation details — which database, which protocol — go on the next layer up. Done this way, diagrams become extensible: you can add a layer for domain-driven design boundaries, or transactional scope, or any other meta-information you want to contrast against the topology.

sections.t: Standards, and when to break them
sections.cap: C4's four Cs: Context (users and external dependencies), Container (deployment boundaries — a good meeting point with operations), Component (the architect's view), Class.
items: **Titles** on every element, unless it's genuinely well known to the audience. Rotate them to stick to the right thing and use space efficiently.
**Lines** thick enough to see. Arrows for direction where flow matters. Different arrowheads may carry different meaning — just be consistent about it.
**Shapes**: no pervasive standard exists. The authors use three-dimensional boxes for deployable artifacts, rectangles for containers, cylinders for databases — and admit there is no key beyond that.

**Colour** is under-used, largely because books were printed in black and white for years. Use it to distinguish artifacts — but **never as the only distinction**, because colourblind viewers lose the meaning entirely. Pair it with distinct iconography, the way crossing lights pair red and green with different figures.
**Keys** whenever shapes could be ambiguous. **An easily misinterpreted diagram is worse than no diagram at all.**
sections.p: Establish a standard for the organisation, and allow reasonable exceptions. Architects break the rules whenever the standard has no good way to express the design — and the alternative is what heavyweight CASE tools produced: elaborate models of simple things, full of details that were noise in that context.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 23: Diagramming Architecture, pp. 423–431. C4 is Simon Brown's; ArchiMate is The Open Group's.
